title: We, Not Me
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane, a fifth-grade teacher whose class is largely below benchmark in oral reading fluency, explains why he moved from teacher read-aloud to FASE reading, a routine from the Teach Like a Champion team. In FASE, which stands for Fluent, Attentive, Social and Expressive, students read short chunks aloud in turn at the teacher's call while the teacher reads about half the text. He rejects extended independent reading for these students because decoding drains the attention they need for comprehension, and finds partner reading and pure read-aloud each lose something. He walks through the four letters in order of importance, putting Social first because reading becomes shared and students ask to read. His practical advice covers explaining why, practising in a small group first, keeping the routine unpredictable, staying positive and rehearsing the text. A closing story about an avoidant reader who now insists on her turn answers the worry that the routine will make struggling readers anxious. Kane is clear that FASE supplements, and does not replace, a repeated reading routine and small-group intervention.
points: Extended independent reading fails a class of weak decoders because their mental energy goes to the words, leaving them tired and unsure what they read.
Cold-calling students to read short chunks makes following along worthwhile, because no one knows when their turn will come.
Reading that is shared builds motivation, so struggling readers begin to ask for their turn and read with more care.
Mixing teacher read-aloud with student chunks, and rereading hard passages, lets the teacher tune comprehension against fluency practice on the fly.
The routine only works with a positive tone, a clear explanation of why, and low-stakes practice in a small group before whole-class use.
quotes: Extended independent reading tends to result in distracted, tired students who don’t know what they just read.
It just felt passive, like reading was something happening to students rather than with students, like something we rush through rather than something we savor.
FASE stands for Fluent, Attentive, Social, and Expressive. It’s a cousin of popcorn reading. Students take turns reading aloud, but with a high degree of teacher control.
The piece I love most about FASE reading is that reading feels shared. Reading isn’t something that happens to students; it’s something we do together.
Students don’t know when they will be called on, so they have an incentive to follow along.
Reading everything aloud myself sends a message that students aren’t capable readers. FASE reading is meant to do the opposite.
Keep the routine a bit unpredictable. I often call on a student in the middle of a paragraph, and I vary the length that students read at once.
It’s no secret to struggling students that they aren’t fluent readers. Hiding that away doesn’t make them more fluent, it only makes their dysfluency invisible.
